label: Treated seed and animal feed
summary: Seed for planting may be coated with a pesticide; in Canada treated seed must be stained a conspicuous colour and labelled 'Do not use for food or feed'. Feed medicated with monensin has killed dogs, horses and guinea fowl, and mouldy grain and feed can carry mould poisons that survive food processing. Feed grain and pet food are made for animals, not people.
signs: Seed or grain stained a bright, unnatural colour, or coated: in Canada any seed treated with a pesticide must be stained or coated so it stands out
Bags, tags or packets reading 'Do not use for food or feed. This seed has been treated with...', with a hazard symbol and a signal word such as Caution, Warning, Danger or Poison
Planters and their hoppers, and empty seed bags: they can hold leftover treated seed and its dust
Feed or premix labelled with a drug name, withdrawal times or warnings such as 'Do not allow dogs, horses, other equines, or guinea fowl access': medicated feed
Grain or feed that is mouldy, discoloured or shrivelled
Stored grain may have been treated with insecticide, or with fumigant pellets or 'ropes' that give off phosphine gas (see Grain bins, hoppers and silos)
Raw, frozen and freeze-dried pet foods and treats can carry Salmonella and Listeria; freezing and drying lower the germs but don't remove them
do: Keep treated seed in its labelled bag, for planting only
Handle treated seed in chemical-resistant gloves, long sleeves and long trousers or coveralls; pour it gently and don't shake out the dust
Pick up spilled treated seed or work it into the soil, and keep it and its dust out of water
Give medicated feed only to the animal named on its label; keep monensin feed away from dogs and horses, which it has killed
Before eating any grain, look it over and throw out anything mouldy, discoloured, shrivelled or dyed; keep the rest dry, cool and free of insects
Wash hands before and after handling pet food, and keep bowls and scoops clean

Feed grain and pet food are made for animals, not people. Sealed, undamaged cans of pet food are heat-sterilised, and in the US must follow the low-acid canning rules meant to leave them free of live germs
dont: Don't eat dyed or treated seed, or feed it to animals, however hungry you or they are
Don't mix treated seed into food grain or feed, or store it in food bins
Don't reuse treated-seed bags for food or feed: dust can stay in them
Don't give livestock feed to dogs, horses or other species unless its label names them
Don't eat or feed mouldy grain or feed: most mould poisons survive food processing
ppe: Chemical-resistant gloves, long sleeves and long trousers or coveralls for treated seed, plus a respirator if the seed tag calls for one

For medicated premix: impervious gloves, protective clothing and dust protection, as the monensin label requires (it says dust mask); a NIOSH-approved N95 seals tightly to the face when fitted properly
firstAid: Swallowed treated seed or medicated premix: treat it as a chemical poisoning (see Chemicals) and keep the bag or tag to show a medic
Premix or seed dust on skin: wash it off with soap and water; in the eyes, see Chemicals

Sick after eating stored grain, feed or pet food: stop eating that batch. Mould poisons can cause vomiting, diarrhoea and, in large aflatoxin doses, life-threatening liver damage; raw and dried pet food can carry Salmonella and Listeria
A dog or horse that ate cattle or poultry feed with monensin can die: take the feed away at once
